questions.prompt: At minute 2 a bar and a fill both have time 2. Why does the strategy see the bar first?
options: Bars always come before fills, whatever their times
The bar was pushed into the queue first, so its tie-breaking counter is smaller
The fill's time is 3, so it comes later
heapq returns events in the order of their kind names
questions.explanation: Events are ordered by time and then by the counter `seq`. The three bars were pushed before any fill, so at equal time 2 the bar has the smaller counter and comes out first.

questions.prompt: What must change to run the same strategy live?
options: The strategy function `on_bar` must be rewritten for live prices
The event queue must be sorted by price instead of time
Nothing: the backtester already sends real orders
The source of bars and the simulated broker are replaced; `on_bar` stays the same
questions.explanation: The strategy only reacts to events. Live, the bars come from the market and the fills from a real broker, but `on_bar` receives the same kind of events in the same time order.

questions.prompt: Why can't the strategy in this loop read a bar from the future?
options: A bar reaches the strategy only when the loop takes it from the queue at its own time
The bars are shifted by one row before the loop starts
The simulated broker deletes future bars
Python's heapq raises an error on future times
questions.explanation: The loop hands out the earliest event each time. A bar for minute 2 is still in the queue while the strategy handles minute 1, so the strategy has no way to see it.
